utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, in any event, the confidential part should be put under seal. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read a short summary of the transcript, i.e., Professor Milos Bojinovic's testimony in English. [In English] Milos Bojinovic was the chief of the agency for population movement and the exchange of material wealth for the Autonomous Region of Krajina, for the agency. He began working in Banja Luka at the agency on July the 1st, 1992. The agency served a humanitarian role for people living in the ARK. It was established to assist any person in need or any person whose life was at risk. Agency activities centred on the two main tasks: Helping people exchange their addresses and facilitating travel. Ethnicity was irrelevant to the agency's function. Several services were offered by the agency, but it was only able to provide transportation and travel-related services due to the war-time circumstances. Bus convoys organised by the agency travelled from Banja Luka to Gradiska and further to Croatia, and from Banja Luka to Vlasic, several times a month. Buses left Banja Luka two or three times per month in convoys usually comprised of two or three buses. Although citizens sought bus transportation to Zagreb and Travnik, the agency could not provide complete transportation to the city cities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If the court deputy approach the Bench

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Individuals leaving Banja Luka were required to present a document proving they had registered out of their place of residence before they could secure the agency's bus transportation. Travellers could obtain the document through the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the police, in the person's respective municipality. Individuals were placed on a list of people scheduled for departure after presenting the document to the agency. After the agency reviewed and finalised its list, the listed individuals would buy tickets, and the agency would hire buses. It did not own its own fleet. Ticket prices were non-negotiable and were fixed by local regulations. All ticket prices were regular bus lines in the region were fixed at an equal value. The agency operative, Bandic and Segrt, would evaluate safety concerns and determine whether the bus convoy would need a police escort. The operatives would submit a report to the agency describing military activity on the route and whether the trip was safe. If agency operatives discovered military activity along the convoy's anticipated route, the convoys were not permitted to leave. Conversely, buses were permitted to leave when no military activity existed along the route. The agency requested police protection whenever its operatives determined a safety risk was nevertheless present, particularly around the line separating the two armies. However, agency operatives escorted the convoys because the travellers would be travelling, regardless of whether a police escort was needed or provided. He never witnessed agency operatives or the police maltreat passengers, nor did he witness personal property or money being extorted, demanded, or taken from boarding passengers. Mr. Bojinovic travelled in the bus convoys on two separate occasions, one trip towards Vlasic and another towards Gradiska. He accompanied the convoy to Gradiska for two reasons. First, he wanted to understand the experience and how passengers felt; second, he felt compelled to escort his Muslim friends to the border. Mr. Bojinovic's convoy trip toward Gradiska was unescorted by police and seemed similar to convoys he previously observed departing. He noticed passengers of various ethnicities on the bus. He saw Muslims, Croats, Slovenians, and Serbs. Uniformed men did not stop the bus and Mr. Bojinovic never observed any mistreatment of passengers. The second convoy Mr. Bojinovic accompanied went to Vlasic, towards Travnik. The convoy consisted of a single bus which contained several passengers from mixed marriages between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Despite the condition on mountain roads, Mr. Bojinovic did not experience anything unusual travelling to Vlasic. The police and the agency operatives escorted the bus, yet Mr. Bojinovic did not observe any passenger mistreatment or illegal activity. The agency closed in December 1992 and the refugee commission continued providing the services previously provided by the agency. Mr. Bojinovic never heard negative comments being made towards the non-Serbian population during his time as chief. Similarly, he never heard Serbian politicians propose limitations against non-Serbians, nor did he ever hear of Serbs seeking to cleanse the area. Mr. Bojinovic never heard people allege the agency was extorting money from non-Serbs. If someone had, in fact, made such allegations, those allegations would be untrue. People were leaving because the war made the area unsafe, not because of ethnic cleansing. And that would be a short summary. At that moment, I would not ask Professor Bojinovic anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written -- your previous testimony in the previous case. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, your evidence is that you held no official position in the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And certainly not a member of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 1D26027, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document that's been uploaded in this case by the Defence which lists members of the Main Board which include many people this Trial Chamber is familiar with, including Mr. Karadzic. We can see, for example, Bozidar Vucurevic, Mladen Nedic, Mico Stanisic, and we also see your name at number 3. So this document shows that you were more than just a candidate for the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But would you ask whether he confirms whether he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yeah, I was just about to do that. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, as I said, this shows that you were more than just a candidate, that you were, in fact, a member of the SDS Main Board, doesn't it -- or you were, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct. I was just a candidate for a member of the Main Board. When you say "more than a candidate," I don't understand that. I was a candidate but I was never elected a member of the Main Board. And you can see it quite clearly. Under 3, Milos Bojinovic, yes, I am here, my name is here, I was a candidate. And that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, it was your words, saying that you were only a candidate when you testified in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So this document lists you as a member of the Main Board, not as a candidate for the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that based on this. If I had been a member of the Main Board, I would have attended meetings throughout the year; however, I did not attend any meetings. This is a list of potential candidates for the positions as members of the Main Board. So this is not an official document. If this were an official document, it would bear a party stamp and you can't see it here, so I believe that everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? Perhaps if it would help if Madam Sutherland would explain the period from which this document originates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't think that that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number P6558, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, sir, it's also your evidence that you were not politically active --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, please, may I be allowed to address the Court? May I react, please? It is very important to look at the date on this document, the date could have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, you stated this is a -- just list of candidates. Would you like to add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This list of candidates could have been drafted on the eve of the establishment of the party and, in official terms, the party was established on the 12th of July, 1990. Up to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will ask more questions. Shall we continue, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, sir, it's also your evidence that you were not politically active in Glamoc municipality; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, you weren't politically active?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said Milan Babic was the first president of the SDS in Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Milan Babic, I'm not familiar with that name. I'm familiar with the family name Babic. After I left Glamoc, I don't know who the president of the municipal SDS board was. Before I left, nobody was president. People just gathered --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and no president had been elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said at transcript page 22824 when you were asked who was the first president of the SDS in Glamoc, you said: "Up until the establishment of the SDS, there was no president. After the SDS was established in 1990, I think it was Milorad Babic. Babic. That's his family name. But I'm not sure about his first name." Now, that's what you did say when you testified previously, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. Let me tell you it is possible --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But in fact --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but a lot of time has passed since then, but I'm not familiar with that at all. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But in fact, Mr. Bojinovic, the first SDS president that was appointed was yourself, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't be the president of something that hadn't been established yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Upon its establishment --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People did hold me in high esteem --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Upon its establishment, you became the first SDS president, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was never --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 25749, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap. Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 25749, and my apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a document of questioning of Radoslav Simidzija on the 11th and 12th of June, 1995. Do you know a person by that name who lived in Glamoc since 1976?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we go to page 11 of the English translation and page 6 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we see there that Mr. Simidzija states that Milos Bojinovic was the first president of Glamoc SDS. And he says in the current chairman, that is 1995, there is a certain Babic from S. Selo. Do you still maintain that you weren't the first SDS president?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, the evidence is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, it's in the record. It's in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You continued your involvement with the SDS when you moved to Banja Luka in July 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure to which question the witness answered "yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, oh, I will clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, do you agree that you were the SDS president in Glamoc in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to explain that. The position of the president of the SDS did not exist before the establishment of the SDS. There was a person who chaired a gathering, where the SDS is discussed, somebody who chairs a gathering. But a president has to be elected and receive a letter of appointment with a stamp of the party. I never received that and I never was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you chaired a gathering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not every gathering, in the early days. Later on, meetings would be chaired by whoever is elected, whoever is chosen. One meeting lasts for about an hour and then the chairperson is chosen. I was not always the chairperson, only when people would choose me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So most specifically, you agree that you chaired some of the meetings, SDS meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You continued your involvement with the SDS when you moved to Banja Luka in July 1992, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand, what do you mean by "you continued your involvement"? I was a member of the SDS but I didn't hold any high positions in the SDS. So clarify what you mean by "continued your involvement." What exactly do I understand by that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said when you testified in the Brdjanin case that you were a member of the SDS throughout?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You knew Nenad Stevandic, did you not, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I know Stevandic only now. I didn't know him then. Only now when Stevandic became a deputy from the SDS party. At that time, I had no idea of his existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, the agency to which you were appointed was an organ of the Autonomous Region of Krajina government, yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Please, now -- because the Assembly of the ARK established the agency. It must have had a government. Somebody had to have jurisdiction over the agency, the Assembly or the government, but it was all within the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: By the latter part of 1992, the work of the agency was basically or almost exclusively organising travel to send people outside Republika Srpska, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. Travel is the last part. Before travel, we've already had occasion to hear that there had been procedures for people to register with the agency, to leave their addresses so that we can put them in contact with people of non-Serb ethnicity so they can come to an arrangement. I must have talked about that before in the Brdjanin case. The agency put people in touch, for instance, Muslims and Croats and -- or Serbs or Slovenes would come to the agency, leave their addresses, and say: I have in Banja Luka such and such an apartment or a house, I would like to swap it for something in Zagreb, Sarajevo, Zenica. And then Serbs would contact us from these areas from which they had fled, leave their addresses, and we would put that up on a board and people would look for appropriate swaps. That was one of the types of assistance the agency provided --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- second, people were able to -- yes, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified in the Brdjanin case that -- you were taken to a document which listed five services that the agency was supposed to offer, and you said that in relation to at least four of them, that you weren't doing that particular -- that you weren't providing that particular service. And in fact, the only thing you were doing was providing the bus service and you were making it possible for people to obtain addresses of other interested persons so they could contact each other. And that's what you said at transcript page 22886. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you say that there were only one or two convoys leaving per month. One witness in the Brdjanin case, that's BT94, said at transcript page 18005 that two or three buses a day were leaving and he witnesses convoying leaving the agency "day-in/day-out." He said that he saw huge crowds next to the workers' centre where that was happening. He said there would always be a throng of people, a multitude of people waiting there, queuing to get out. This, what I've just said to you in relation to his evidence, represents the reality of the situation, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is my comment required?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, not a comment but an answer to my question. This was the reality of the situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's not that. The person who said there was a multitude of people doesn't understand anything. Do you know what it means, a multitude of people? A multitude of people of lined bodies which do not move, so it cannot be a multitude of people. About the long lines, where would they fit? There was no room for such queues. People came normally to our offices --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, you said you were receiving a --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I say?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were receiving 500 requests a day, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, impossible. Where would 500 applications come from when it was impossible to organise transport every week? It all depended on the security situation. There was a war going on, people. We cannot drive people through war zones. It could have been once, twice, or three times a month, three times a month max, not four, which means not every week. And there was only one bus, perhaps two or three depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once were there five or six buses, as far as I remember. I want to use this opportunity to answer another question --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I was asked how many people in total left --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will ask you the questions and you will answer them to the best of your ability.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to 500 requests a day, I would refers Your Honours and the accused to P03857.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you -- that people paid the -- this is in your testimony, that people paid the bus fare to leave which was regulated by town laws and you said it was the same fee as other regular bus lines applied. But there were no other bus lines, were there, because Putnik and Atlas Travel had been shut down by the ARK Crisis Staff, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was shut down. It's possible that in the area of AR Krajina there was transport available. But the price of the ticket was regulated by certain regulations --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who gave you this fee that you had to charge? Who gave you the amount of the fee that you had to charge?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one gave it. Regulations existed. The Official Gazette and our secretariat simply followed the regulations. It wasn't an aunt or a grandpa from the municipality who came and told me: Mr. Bojinovic, this is how you're going to do it. No, it's not done like that. There are regulations, the Official Gazette, the secretariat, which follows all that and everything is done in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now you said that it wasn't an exorbitant amount; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by exorbitant price or a low price or a middle price. I don't know. There is a standard price, the standard price that you cannot go outside of much, either below or above. For example, the price of the ticket from Banja Luka to Gradiska was known from beforehand. The price of the ticket from Banja Luka via Gradiska, for example, up to the border with Croatia was a bit more expensive and so on and so forth. So when I say the fees were standard, standard for a certain route and the routes were longer or shorter and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: People were interviewed by the Special Rapporteur Mazowiecki, who said they were forced to pay a fee of 300 Deutschemarks to the agency per person to leave for a Muslim-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you asked me a question? Please ask a question so I can answer with a yes or no or make a comment. If it's just a comment of yours, I'm left waiting and I'm not sure what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This -- you're aware that people were paying up to 300 Deutschemarks to leave on your -- through your agency, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, no, no. That's malevolence of the person who told Mazowiecki or whoever that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 11511, please. And if we could go to page 3 in the middle of the page, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, this is what the Special Rapporteur said, that both the local authorities and the immigration agency in Banja Luka organised their displacement, this is 14.000 people that -- that were in the city of Travnik, and they said: "... and that some of them had paid a fee of up to 300 Deutschemarks per person to leave for a Muslim-controlled territory. They were driven towards the front lines, but were obliged to leave the bus several kilometres before reaching it and to cross the combat zone as best they could. En route they were repeatedly beaten, robbed, subjected to various forms of harassment and in some cases raped or shot." So are you saying these people were lying to the Special Rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have asked me a big question. You read out from a document. Which people, which rapporteur, and specifically could you summarise that a bit, please, so that we may simplify matters? Please don't introduce such big issues here. I can see that there are some numbers here, 19.000 people, 14.000 displaced people, 300 Deutschemarks. Please ask me one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, those figures -- the document states that the city of Travnik had a population of 19.000, has now had to accommodate an additional 14.000 displaced people. And that many of the people that the Special Rapporteur interviewed told him that both the local authorities and an immigration agency in Banja Luka organised their displacement and that some of them had paid a fee of up to 3.000 [sic] Deutschemarks per person to leave for a Muslim-controlled territory. Now, you know that people were paying these large sums of money to leave your agency -- through your agency, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, I shall answer in view of the figures. As for the people who lived in Travnik, I don't know. How many people Travnik planned to accommodate there as refugees, again I'm not aware of that. No one ever told me this. As for people paying 300 Deutschemarks to the agency, that's not true. Who they told that and when, I wouldn't know. With what goal they said that, I don't know, but they didn't say it in honesty. It's easy to say anything once you leave the area of Banja Luka and go over there, it's easy to say anything, but that's not true, it's not correct, and it's not fair, so I deny all of this. It's not true that anyone ever paid 300 Deutschemarks to the agency because it was not necessary. I mean, what was 300 Deutschemarks at the time? Where would poor people get so much money at the time? Please, come on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, there's no question, is there, that the people who were leaving on the buses were mostly Muslims. That's what you said when you testified in the Brdjanin case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly Muslims, but there were others too. There were Croats, there were Serbs, mixed marriages. Who was leaving and for what reasons, I wouldn't know. What was up to me was to make it possible for people to leave in a normal way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said at transcript page 22889 when you were asked who the majority of people were leaving -- who were the majority of people leaving Banja Luka, you said: "The majority were Muslims." And you went on at page 22899 to say: "These people were not from Banja Luka only, not exactly the way it was, that Muslims were leaving Banja Luka en masse. We were contacted by people from Banja Luka and from places where conflicts were nearby."

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you were asked who was leaving you said at transcript page 22806: "There were people from mixed marriages too, here and there the occasional mixed marriage between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, whoever felt that it was safer for them to go to Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not to Travnik, excuse me. Only once one bus went to Travnik because leaving for Travnik was unsafe. Why?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there was a war going on between the Croats and the Muslims -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was your testimony at page 22806. We can bring it up if you really want to see that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were asked who was leaving --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- that is, which ethnicities were leaving on the buses, and you said and your answer is: "My apologies. There were people from mixed marriages, too, here and there, the occasional mixed marriage between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. Whoever felt that it was safer for them to go to Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was exactly to Travnik, but outside of the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, that is to say Banja Luka, but not to Travnik. I have said it again now. Whoever believed that he was threatened, the agency offered him an opportunity, and for Travnik there was a single bus. We wouldn't allow people to go to the combat zone. It was dangerous for those who were driving and for the people who were leaving there. We were not so inhumane that we would send people away to get killed. If need be, I will clarify that the family of a colleague of mine which insisted to go to Travnik, I didn't allow them to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the family waited for almost a month --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, I have limited time. I need to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you referred to your time, I think you passed your time that you suggested. How long --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- how much more do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I need another -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I wasn't aware that I'd reached my time. I need another 15 minutes. I think I could safely wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, despite the numbers involved and despite your official role in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, you professed to be completely mystified about why people were leaving. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I claim. I'm not claiming that I have no idea why they were leaving. I know perfectly well why they were leaving and I have explained it. They were leaving because of uncertainty. Both the Serbs and the Croats and the Muslims and the Slovenes, they did leave. Why were they leaving? Everywhere where the war broke out, there were unofficial elements which were out of control and in order for people to be secured, to be safe, somebody had to take care of them. In my Glamoc, Serbs used to kill one another among themselves --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you mentioned in the beginning the three --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- we're discussing now people leaving from Banja Luka. You were asked what happened in Banja Luka during the time you were chief of the agency to make the Muslims feel unsafe and you said: "I don't know. It was peaceful in Banja Luka." And that's transcript pages 22898, line 23, through to 22990, line 3. Some of the evidence that we've heard in this case is Mr. Andjelko Grahovac, who said that -- who knew that hundreds of small businesses belonging to non-Serbs were blown up at night in Banja Luka. And he was aware that thousands of Muslims and Croats were evicted from their apartments, sometimes by creating fear in them and sometimes by people breaking into their apartments and throwing them out of their apartments in Banja Luka. Internationals reported explosions and machine-gun fire 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber and the accused, that's P02939.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You didn't hear about any of these things that were going on in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mr. Andjelko Grahovac stated is his statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I did not see these things -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- I'm asking you about the incidents that I referred to. Did you or did you not hear and see these things happening?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see these things happening. And one could hear that people were disturbed, that they were leaving enterprises. You could hear that in conversation with simple people, but as for me, seeing something and being convinced, no. That 100 firms were blown up, no. That would mean that all of Banja Luka was razed to the ground and Banja Luka is still standing. There were no combat operations at all. I had been in Banja Luka since 1990. I didn't see that. I had colleagues who worked together with me in high school and to this day there are Croats and Muslims who work there. If you would like me to do so, I will tell you their names. I don't know about this. I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what this is. People went because they were feeling unsafe, but they didn't -- yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- we have evidence in this case that non-Serbs had lost their jobs, they were being harassed and then marginalised and they feared persecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber and the accused that's P03857.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has received evidence that ARK leaders, and particularly the president of the ARK Crisis Staff, publicly demeaned and dehumanised Muslims and called for their expulsion. Do you claim that you were totally oblivious to this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present in a situation when anyone was abused, mistreated, thrown out of a company, or anything. I claim this with my full responsibility, that in high school that I went to after the agency, people remained in their posts and worked on, both Croats and Muslims. If you'd like, I will give you their names. Some were principals for two terms of office, please. So I did not see what you are putting to me now. No, I cannot lie, I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Some of the evidence in this case, Mr. Kupresanin heard from Serbs that Brdjanin said that only a thousand Muslims could stay in Banja Luka. Mr. Grahovac again talked about a percentage of Muslims and Croats that Brdjanin said would be allowed to stay in the Bosanska Krajina, and the rest would leave. Mr. Erceg spoke about repeated statements of the president of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, public statements, some in very ugly forms, that Muslims had to go. He said Brdjanin did make those statements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please -- I would like to have the statements of these witnesses literally and specifically quoted to the witness and read out to him because if you just make a sort of mishmash like this, then it leaves a different impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't paraphrasing the evidence. I can read out what Mr. Grahovac and Mr. Erceg say in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure which would be the best way, but the witness will be better off if you deal with one by one or just put your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was -- it was actually the -- those witnesses that I just read about were talking about the one issue, and that is Brdjanin saying that people had to leave. Only a small percentage would be allowed to stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, so it's your evidence that you weren't aware of Mr. Brdjanin saying that only a small number -- a small percentage would be allowed to say. That's your position, isn't it, that you were never aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear from him when he said that, but people did report that he was saying something to that effect. But I did not hear it from his specifically because I was not present in a situation, if something like this was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And whatever he said, that's for him to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so when you were asked -- when you were asked why -- what would it be to make Muslims feel unsafe and you said "I don't know," it never occurred to you that this might be a factor in people leaving their homes, their positions, and the lives they had built?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I know that many Croats and Muslims stayed. It all depended on the mental structure of the people, their emotions and so on. I think that this is a question that I'm not competent enough to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Let me take you to one example.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter number 25743, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is an article which was published in "The Guardian" on the 29th of September, 1992. It was an article written by Ian Traynor. And if we can go to paragraph 5, we can see that Mr. Vukic -- Dr. Vukic says -- he's an obstetrician and he recently stated no Muslim or Croat woman would be allowed to give birth in his hospital. And he also said that -- he quotes Radoslav Brdjanin and says that he just announced "that Banja Luka has room for only 1.000 Muslims. The other 29.000 would have to go 'one way or another.'" "One way or another" being in quotes. You're living in Banja Luka at this time, in September 1992, weren't aware of these public threats that were being made by Dr. Vukic and Brdjanin which were reported in the British press?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One clarification. We heard in translation that what Brdjanin said, that Vukic actually told that to the journalist and it's not so. [In English] Who quoted Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You may ask -- you may clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But it is a part of question, not a part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, this article states that Radoslav Vukic said recently - this is in September 1992 - no Muslim or Croat woman would be allowed to give birth in his hospital. That's the first thing. The second thing this article states is that Radoslav Brdjanin, who was head of the regional war committee who has just announced "that Banja Luka has room for only 1.000 Muslims. The other 29.000 would have to go 'one way or another.'" Now, as I asked you, you were living in Banja Luka at the time, in September 1992, you didn't hear these public statements being made by Dr. Vukic and Brdjanin? You did hear them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you say --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear them, but if something like that was said by Dr. Vukic, then that was not nice. He had to have taken the Hippocratic oath. If he did say that, I would not agree. It shouldn't be done. However, you say here Vukic told Brdjanin and Brdjanin told Vukic and so on and so forth. I don't know what they told one another.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I didn't say that --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as I man, I have this position that -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I didn't say that, Mr. Bojinovic. I specifically said --

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm receiving interpretation, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to paragraph 8 it says there: "Ten days ago, 150 [sic] people paid 100 Deutschemarks a head to the agency for the final stage of their transfers, after having surrendered their property in Banja Luka and boarded buses to the Croatian border." Now, again this is a figure being paid to your agency of 100 Deutschemarks a head. Do you still deny that people were having to pay these amounts of between 100 and 300 Deutschemarks, some of the people that went through your agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were not forced to pay between 100 and 300 Deutschemarks but the price of the ticket as it was set because there would be consequences for us, the agency, if we were working like that. The authorities functioned in Banja Luka. We couldn't work independently. It wasn't like this. 100 or 300 Deutschemarks, it's a lot of money. People did not have that and the poor people carried with them what they had. I personally gave my own money to the Glamoc Muslims and they cried when they realised what it was and they offered me -- please, they offered me: No, you take it, you need more, and it will be easier for me to fend for myself here because this is my people. So that was my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, I wish to take you to two other portions in this document and that's on page 2, the second paragraph. We see here it says: "Foreign relief" -- it's reported in this article that: "Foreign relief workers in the town are staggered by the levels of hatred, violence, and victimisation they are now encountering every day." And that is the Muslims encountering every day this -- these levels of hatred, violence, and victimisation. You didn't see this, living in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who could have seen such hatred in the street. How can you know from someone's face if he were a Serb, a Croat, a Muslim, a Jew, a Pole, and how can you see on his face hatred against other people? For me, this question makes no sense. I cannot answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And lastly, the second-to-last paragraph on page 2, the portion -- now it starts: "Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader who came here last Friday to try to sweet talk Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen, told The Guardian the same day that 'Banja Luka is a peaceful town.' The night before, Serbian special units sealed off the district of Hiseta and ordered all the residents out of their houses, barking their orders through megaphones. Local Muslims thought they were headed for Manjaca or Trnopolje, but it was a false alarm - just another exercise in intimidation." Now, again, something else that you weren't aware of that was happening in the town that you were living in, of Muslims being intimidated and taken out of their houses?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I said you're not aware -- that this is something else that you're also not aware of, people being intimidated by their houses being searched and being thrown out of their houses?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw this. I was not looking on. When did that happen, how did it happen? No, I had my job, I'm a family man, I had to take care about that, and I tried to help the people who addressed me. And whether there were some paramilitary formations and some incidents, I didn't see that. Banja Luka is a big town, let me tell you. I cannot be simultaneously in all places where possible excesses were taking place. So when you say "were you aware," it's a little bit -- well, was I aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, I'll put it to you, it's disingenuous of you to say that you don't know why thousands of non-Serbs are seeking your agency to leave Banja Luka when all of this is going on in Banja Luka at the time that you're living there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have told you this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say why -- that he didn't know why. He said that he knew quite well why they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been explained that people were leaving because they were feeling unsafe, not only the Muslims, though. The majority were the Muslims, that is correct. But it was not just the Muslims. There were the Croats also, fewer, and the Serbs, also fewer. There were the Slovenes as well. There were people from mixed marriages. And now it's insisted here that in Banja Luka there was a general widespread persecution of Muslims. I did not notice that. I'm sorry, excuse me, but I did not notice that that was so. In high school where I worked, people continued working, the Croats and the Muslims. A Croat woman used to be the principal for eight years. A secretary was -- there were two and now there's another one who is a Muslim, the secretary. The colleagues who were teaching there. So what are we talking about here? This was the high school, a public institution, where other intellectuals worked side by side with me without any problems. I have a list with me, the list of persons who can be called here to testify and to confirm whether this is correct or not. There were people who stayed on and worked on in high school. There are my friends, Muslims, whom I helped. So if I need to present all this to you, if these people need to be consulted, you can find a way to do that. But to create such a picture like this, that there was a general persecution, almost a massacre, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, most of it has been read out, but if you do admit it, I would ask you to consider for the weight of the document how there is absolute complete absence of attribution of any information to named people in that article. It is really quite a remarkable piece of journalism actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question, I was wondering why this document is to be admitted through this witness. Contradiction, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he -- I didn't go through his testimony, but did he contradict in his testimony what is -- with respect to what is described in this article?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'd asked him whether he was aware of these things occurring. He said it wasn't -- he was living in Banja Luka at the time these things were occurring. I think in order for you to -- sorry, Mr. Tieger wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, when he said it went to the weight of the document, is basically agreeing that it's impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, for the purpose of impeachment, I think the -- given that the all most relevant parts were read out to the transcript, the Chamber is of the view that it's not necessary to admit this. We'll not admit it. And you're done with your --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I appreciate Your Honours' indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much do you need, Mr. Karadzic, for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Ten minutes, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll ask the audio unit whether we have sufficient tape for ten minutes. If yes, we'll continue. We have only 11 minutes, but are you confident that -- otherwise we'll rise for ten minutes and then we can continue, and then after which we'll have a 20-minute break for the preparation of the next witness. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- we'll take a brief adjournment. We'll resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Bojinovic, could I ask you to give the name of some prominent Muslims and Croats who stayed in Banja Luka throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to give you the names of my colleagues who were all professors at the Banja Luka grammar school, and that grammar school has a tradition spanning over a hundred years. Azijada Bera, who was the grammar school secretary. The current secretary is Majda Pucar who is also Muslim. Professor Begic, who had joined the grammar school to teach physics. Jasna Maric, the teacher of art history. Amira Zmiric, who is the teacher of German. She worked at the school and now is a member of the faculty at the university and so on and so forth. There are a few more people who I used to see around town, but let me tell you I have forgotten their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe that Vukic and Brdjanin proffered those words as their official position? How would Radic have reacted? Would he have accepted that as a political stance?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Radic is a gentleman and he would not have accepted such a policy, but it is possible [Realtime transcript read in error "policy"] that Brdjanin and Vukic said something to that effect on some occasion. I'm not denying that, it is possible, but I did not hear them say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Probably line 11 should say "it is possible" instead of "it's policy." Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is possible that they said that. Did the local authorities and Radic implement things of the kind that are ascribed to Brdjanin and Vukic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Banja Luka was a peaceful city during Radic's term of office and chapeau to him for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to call for a paper to be placed on the ELMO. You saw that report in which it is stated that Travnik had 19.000 inhabitants and that it had to receive an additional 14.000 refugees. Could you please read from the document, how many inhabitants did Travnik have in 1991 according to that year's census?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be zoomed in, please. [In English] Please, could you enlarge it, could you augment it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please tell us what was the total number of inhabitants in Travnik and how many of them were Croats, how many were Serbs, how many were Yugoslavs, and how many were others?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the first line.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A total 70.000, Croats 24.000, Muslims 31.000, Serbs 7.000, Yugoslavs 3.600, others 1.000, and then those who did not declare their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Others, 1.093?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the information that we heard about 19.000 is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it's not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document to be marked for identification pending translation. Actually, the only thing that needs to be done is to transliterate it into the Latinic script. The rest is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is this from, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is from an official publication, the Serbian version albeit, of the last census which was carried out in 1991. You can double-check the information in the Croatian version. The same list was compiled by the Republic of Croatia, which was not its call but still it did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives MFI D4179, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Bojinovic, the indictment against me alleges that we expelled people and forced them to leave, and we can see that people had to collect some certificates, to pay for their ticket, to wait to be placed on a list. Could the two things be reconciled? Did they actually ask to be allowed to leave or did we chase them out?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not force anybody to leave. People who felt the need to leave came to us for help. It was not us who approached them; it was the other way around. They gained enough trust in the agency because those who had left before them sent them a word that they were safe and that they could travel. That's my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any feedback from the people whom you had helped to travel?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a lot of feedback, especially from my fellow citizens from Glamoc who were of Muslim ethnicity. They called me from Sweden, from Paris. And when I go to Glamoc, where I have my apartment, I get together with me -- with them, and we are very glad that the war is behind us, that we are still living, and that we can get together and socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were quoted back statements from some witnesses about the distribution of weapons among the Serbs. Did the Serbs respond to mobilisation calls or did they have their own paramilitary formations? And I'm talking about Glamoc.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Glamoc is concerned, I don't know anything about the distribution of weapons that would go beyond official channels. The soldiers in the Glamoc Brigade were mobilised when that was needed. They received weapons. And as for paramilitary formations and some special distributions of weapons, I don't know anything about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now my last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, the last question was very leading. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us in view of the fact that it was alleged that you were a member of various boards and so on and so forth, were you earmarked to become a member of the board and when were the first elections for the real board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population of Glamoc expected me to become politically active; however, they were aware of my character. I'm a poet more than a career person, so I never accepted any of the positions that were offered to me. And I must say that some very good and high positions were offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When were the real elections for the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was only after the SDS was set up in Sarajevo on the 12th of June. That's when the Main Board was elected, and I was disregarded for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did we call those groups of people that assisted in the setting up of the party? You just mentioned the word.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Groups of people who helped --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned initiative boards?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, initiative boards. This actually means the beginning, when things start being created, when an initiative is launched. So the initiative boards were those that alerted us to the imminent danger to which we had to react instead of just sitting idle and watching chaos brewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any of those initiative boards?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Because I knew or I realised that in Bosnia-Herzegovina things were beyond control and that the situation was -- would breed problems. And I spoke to everybody, not only Serbs, also to Croats and Muslims, in the grammar school. I urged them to be proactive to avoid the repetition of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, could somebody consider you a president if you were a member of the initiative board or steering committee?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how people are, they believe you are a president as soon as you have a position although that was never official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Bojinovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Bojinovic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I would like to thank you for your invitation, for the confidence that you placed in me, for your patience, and I would like to ask you to forgive me if I did not abide by your rules. I'm a poet, I write literature books. Once again, thank you. I wish you a lot of success in your work and a lot of health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. We'll resume at 11.33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, good morning. We're joined during this session by Goran Petronijevic, who is the co-ordinator of our Defence team in Belgrade. And I would -- we were planning on just having he and I here, but we're also going to use some videos with this witness and he and I aren't very good at that. So we would wonder if it would be okay if we could have an additional person in the courtroom during this period which would be our case manager, Mr. Stevanovic, to operate the videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, no observations, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's granted. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say something, Mr. Witness, after having made the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said, I've been saying for 20 years what has been done to my life and what sort of lies are being spread here, and still you never called me, and that the Mothers of Srebrenica asked me to testify in Sarajevo. It's not my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear your evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an error in the transcript. The witness said that the Mothers of Srebrenica prevented him, together with the authorities in Sarajevo, prevented him from testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said so, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you understand you are testifying under certain protective measures, that is, you will be called by pseudonym, which is KW-12, not referring to your real name, and your image will not be broadcast outside this courtroom. And whenever we discuss your identity, we'll go into private session so that the others, i.e., the other people outside this courtroom cannot follow who you are. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So whenever you want to talk about something that may reveal your identity, please notify us in advance so that we can go into private session. Do you also understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Yes, it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to put a pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up 1D09534, not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if your name is under this number?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives document number D4180, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters wanted to suggest something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters just want to ask the witness again not to start replying while Mr. Karadzic is still speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you understand that, Witness? Since Mr. Karadzic and you are speaking the same language, so there needs to be some pause between the question and the answers for the interpreters to conclude their interpretation. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, were you a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You started answering again too soon. Could you briefly describe what happened during the war from the beginning of April to the 28th of May, 1992. In your area, were there any clashes in April, any skirmishes, and between who?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, there were some between paramilitary units, Arkan's men, on one hand, and Naser Oric and his men, his army, as they were known at the time; and there were a couple of villages that were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was the outcome of these clashes? Were there any losses? What transpired between them?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There was one ambush set in Potocari where these Arkan's men were killed, everybody knows that, and then there was the mopping up, the cleansing, of Cumavici, which is a village. And there was one ambush in Zeleni Jadar under Osmace. Osmace is a road that leads to Osmace village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the population of these two villages, Cumavici and Gniona?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Those were majority Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who set these two ambushes in Zeleni Jadar and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: In Potocari, Naser Oric and Hakija Meholjic, Mujo Mandzo organised this ambush. How shall I explain it? I'm just trying to explain briefly so you can understand. That ambush was set in Potocari when they killed this Arkan's men. Hakija Meholjic, Mujo Mandzo and Naser Oric were the leaders around whom their people gathered and they organised this ambush in Potocari. Whereas the ambush in Zeleni Jadar, near Sinan's shop, was organised by the men under commander Skraljivode [phoen] and the first commander of that group was Akif. He set an ambush there to intercept an army convoy that was going towards Srebrenica, they killed some people, they slit their throats, and they hanged them. They hanged the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this Akif Ustic?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President, what his real surname was. After so many years -- in that area, I remember only where my own house was. At that time I knew where his house was, but I didn't know his surname. But it's somewhere around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which troops did they ambush?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, it was the JNA. They wore those olive-green-grey uniforms, as we called them SMB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen right at the place where you enter Bratunac, on the 2nd or 3rd May, involving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: When you enter Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the place called Hranca. If you were not there, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There was shooting around Hranca and Glogova. It's about 2 or 3 kilometres from Bratunac. But to tell you the truth, I didn't know the details at that time, I wasn't there. We were in Hranca later in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anything dramatic happen on the 8th of May; and if so, what was it and how did it affect your area?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: You mean 1992, on the 8th of May. It had a strong impact on us residents of Bratunac. That was when Goran Zekic was killed. He was a member of some sort of Presidency in Sarajevo. I have no idea. Maybe he was SDA or some other party. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what was his occupation normally?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President, what he was. He was a teacher or a politician, a professor. I don't know exactly what his position was. All I know was that he was on the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened after that? What did the Serb police demand? Could you describe the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That's a leading question, and I just want to be -- just to make that note of caution with this witness, that Dr. Karadzic should avoid leading the witness. This is one of the first leading questions, but I just mark it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "What happened after that?" Is that a leading question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, no, "what did the Serb police demand," presupposing that there was a demand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If you could tell us what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will ask Mr. Karadzic to reformulate his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said it had caused tensions, but can you describe the chain of events after the 8th of May? What was happening and were you somehow involved in these events?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The 10th May came after that, when we were rounded up in Bratunac. I need to know where to start from. On the 8th of May, that man was killed in Potocari. I came back from Potocari. In Bratunac, on the 9th of May, it was quiet and peaceful. I'm talking about 1992. On the 10th of May, they -- our own neighbours attacked us, rounded us up, and took us to the football-pitch in Bratunac, all of us, Muslims, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have a good insight into the events before the 8th of May? You mentioned those two villages and two ambushes.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: In Gniona and Cumavici, I saw those decapitated bodies and the heads on the ground. I went to that area to bring my ex-wife, and the first time they did not let us go through to Ruovci [phoen], and that's the first time we heard about Gniona. Naser Oric surrounded the Serb people, asked them to turn over their weapons, guaranteeing their security, and then he captured those people, killed some, including some policemen, I knew one of them, and one other man from Lehovici, who captured this policeman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast. He has to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I can see that we are going down the road of this witness testifying about crimes allegedly committed by the ABiH against Serbs. This is the second answer which purports to describe those sorts of events, and I just want to at this point caution Dr. Karadzic and raise this as a potential issue. In my submission, evidence of crimes against Serbs is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I think that would be contrary to everything that has taken place in Krstic, Popovic, Blagojevic, and Tolimir trials with respect to Srebrenica events. The background of the conflicts in that area including attacks against Serb civilians has been an integral part of the evidence in the case and to understanding what happened in 1995 and as well as 1993. So it seems to me that this is different than crimes against Serbs in other aspects of our case that we have been -- that has been excluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Might I just make one observation, which is that we are talking here about 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation, that background material is relevant to the case; however, I'd like to emphasise that we are not -- the Chamber is going -- proposed to hear the evidence on the basis of tu quoque -- not to hear the evidence on the basis of tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Excellencies, but I'm only interested in the chain of events which led to other events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, it's not clearly recorded in the transcript where the heads that had been cut off were posted and what happened with the policeman on the spit.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The heads in Zeleni Jadar below Osmace near Sinan's shop, below and above the road, they were on the staffs or staves, depending on how you call them, they were placed on those staffs. And as for the policemen it's Cumavici and Gniona, two places one next to the other, two villages. Cumavici is on the hill, and Gniona is a bit - how should I put it? - in the valley, down below. If you look from there you can see into the neighbouring village. And in Cumavici, the policeman was burnt. Amir personally used to know him before that and Amir asked him: Well, the time comes for me to pay the fee. Whether the policeman was a traffic policeman who stopped him previously and asked him to pay a speed -- gave him a speeding ticket, but he was roasted on a -- on the spit. And I was present there and I know what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not been recorded, "the spit," but we'll manage. Thank you. So this was done after they had handed over their weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now please help us with this: Was Glogova the subject of a request for the delivery of weapons and what happened around the village of Glogova before --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You told us a little while ago that you were taken to the stadium on the 10th. Don't tell us who, but was anyone of your family members taken with you and did anyone stay in the village?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: My mother --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to say who. You can just say --

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: My mother and my 4-year-old son stayed there, and I and my father were taken to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the stadium were you arrested; and if so, who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: (redacted) and also what was done because it could affect --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were you taken there?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I was taken to the Vuk Karadzic primary school from the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us how they treated you there and who did that? Who was doing what? How many persons were arrested and taken to the school and who was doing what? How were these people treated?

utterances.speaker: KW12
