utterances.text: When I got to the school with my father, in the gym there was a man called Bane and another one called the Macedonian. I also found several people on the left-hand side as I entered the school who were lying down on the floor. My father was also told to lie down, and it lasted like that until the dark. Then another group of people were brought, and the locals, the Serbs, whom we knew because we had been living together with them, some were nice, others argued. And then later they told this Bane and the Macedonian how and what, who should be beaten up, who should be killed, and that happened on the 10th in the evening. They began beating us, killing us. They killed this one man. I can't tell you the numbers, but in my presence around 20 people or so were killed. And I learned and I was told at the time that these people had been Seselj's men, the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha, the White Eagles. Okay. I see it's recorded now. And please tell us, you said that people ordered this because they wanted to settle their previous accounts with their acquaintances, they had some unresolved matters; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did this arrest of yours end and the suspicion that it was you who had shot, how did it all end?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: It was on the 12th -- let me just explain. Please listen to me, everyone. On the 10th of May we were brought to the football-pitch, on the 10th in the afternoon. From the football-pitch I was brought to the gym at around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m. In the evening while we were lying there and everything, whatever you call it, this roll-call started, the locals would come and say: Get me this guy. And then the local wouldn't beat him or kill him, but it was this Bane or the Macedonian who did that. Another thing, all the way until the 12th of May, 1992, the two days and two nights that I spent there, this Bube came to my door and told me, as we were talking, and he said: Neighbour Joska, here's a beer and a coffee, you're still alive and I'll be seeing you. So around 450 of us who would be selected and numbered, around 450 people would be taken for exchange. And we were taken to Pale then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 5 it says: Neighbour Joska, was he neighbour Bube or what was his name?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Bube Ristanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you understand this as being pardoned or that you were no longer a suspect?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I believe that I was pardoned because perhaps he had an unclear conscience because he probably realised that I wasn't the one who had shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your father joined to the people who were transported to Pale?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how were you treated in Pale? Did you have access to water, food, and were you provided with any medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: As for Pale and our arrival there, I can't say anything bad. I can just say good, that I want to thank all the policemen and the hospital. If these people hadn't jumped immediately and taken me, I would have died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You arrived in a bad shape; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I arrived in a bad shape. I was all cut. No one ever put any bandages on me in Bratunac until I arrived up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you provided with medical care?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, immediately. The doctors were there and military police and ordinary police, and no one can say to me that anyone was beaten in Pale. We had better security than in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, are you all right to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm all right, Judge, but you cannot understand me. These moments, all of this, to this day when it's the exact date, I have health problems. And these key questions have an impact on me. For me it's something - how should I tell you? - I don't know, I don't know how to describe that. But all right, I'll stand it. I've withstood worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whenever you find it necessary, please let us know, we'll have a break at any time. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you crying and are you disturbed because of these memories?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Pale --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 45 minutes. We'll resume at five to 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.09 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll try and not to dwell upon the most painful subjects. When were you exchanged and where?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: On the 13th of May, 1992, I was taken from Pale to Cekrcici, that's a village where I was exchanged; and from there I was taken to Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 40115 and can we go into private session. I believe that the document has already been admitted under a P number. But before we proceed, could we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can you briefly tell us what happened to you before you returned to Srebrenica, where were you and how did you finally return to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: From Visoko, when I recovered, I was offered by TO commanders to stay and join the TO units in Visoko. That was offered to us from Bratunac. Some people stayed. A majority of us decided to go to Tuzla. With the help of the Croatian army - and they were known as HOS forces - who had arrived from Kakanj, we were exchanged, but it was not Sarajevo who exchanged us, it was the Croats who exchanged us for some Serbs. And then from Visoko and Kakanj we arrived in Tuzla, across Ozren mountain, and we arrived in Banovici. From Banovici we were sent to various schools. I was sent to the school in Djurdjevik together with my father and many other people. In the meantime, in Djurdjevik, where a refugee camp was set up, the 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade that had arrived from Croatia under the command of Nurif Rizvanovic arrived in the hotel in Zivinice. I learnt from other natives of Bratunac and other people whom I knew, I learned they were at the Hotel Zlaca. And that's how I went from the school in Djurdjevik, together with a young lad whose family name was Civis, on foot to Zlaca and I reported to the 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about that brigade, where did it go? When did you arrive home?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: My first encounter with weapons and the first attack we carried out was in Stevici village near Ozren. A relay was destroyed in 1992 and it was held by the Serbs. That first night we went for something that would be training to get used to the fire and war activities. We spent an entire week there. When we returned to the hotel in Zlaca, Nurif Rizvanovic assigned some 20 of us to go to Tinja. In my statement I already stated - and I'm going to repeat before you - that Tinja was in the hands of the JNA and they didn't wear camouflage uniforms, but normal olive-drab uniforms of the army of the former Tito's Yugoslavia. We had an operation there. We repelled the troops. We destroyed two lorries on the road leading from Tinja to Srebrenik or something like that. On that bridge there we destroyed two military lorries. We also took some prisoners, Serbs. Two Serbs were put on a bus. Those Serbs were beaten all the way to the Zlaca hotel. I omitted to say one thing. The 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade was a unit to which people were selected who had survived a hell, like, for example, I did in Bratunac. Those were special people who had seen Seselj's men and White Eagles killing people and doing things like that. The 16th Eastern Brigade was under the command of Taran, Alija Muskic and Senad Hodzic who was the commander of the police in Bratunac. They told us: If you want to enjoy a better treatment in the unit, like was enjoyed by five platoons, each about 20 men strong, and they were known as Kondors and you could join them only after you had completed training or that you, by Taran and Osmanovic Adil, if you were selected by them you would be trained and only then could you join one of those platoons. And you had to complete a job in front of Medo Jakupovic, you had to slit the throat of one Serb in order to join one of those units. That's the job before you had to complete before your superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether we are talking about two paramilitary formations or are we talking about the White Eagles and you thought they were Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Mr. President, at that time in Bratunac, rumour has it that those were White Eagles and that they were Seselj's men. I don't know whether there was any other kind of information about anybody else. I don't know exactly. Rumour had it that Arkan's men were there as well, as well as the White Eagles. But, however, when things were happening in the Bratunac gym, when people were being killed and beaten, all that involved the White Eagles, i.e., Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The two lorries that you destroyed, were there any troops in those lorries? Were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, there were troops who were sitting in the back, but those lorries were hit by the so-called RPGs, the big rocket-launcher that they had brought back from Croatia, the RPG.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What happened next? How many people put up their candidacy to join the Kondors and how big that unit and how independent it was?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There were people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It was developing into a leading question. It just survived not being one, if Dr. Karadzic be careful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there were 200 men?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Mr. President, there were 200 men, there were Kondors in black uniforms. They -- and in the 16th Muslim Brigade there was a group of over 200 men who were known as Sarenci [phoen], they had special camouflage uniforms, green berets, and Kalashnikov machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did you arrive then and when?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Then we went -- and we are talking about the time when we returned from Tinja; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, when did you arrive home?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I went to a place called Miljanovci, on the road from Zvornik to Tuzla, and we spent a couple of days there. We were told that we should attack a hilltop called Vis, which is on the left-hand side from Miljanovci as you enter Miljanovci from Zvornik. We were also told that we would be helped by the units from Tuzla, which were known at the time as the Dragon of Bosnia. They were going to help us with tanks and mortars and we were supposed to launch an infantry attack in order to take Vis. When we attacked Vis, they did not help us, there were no tanks, there were no mortars, so we had to withdraw. During that withdrawal, we spent a night in Miljanovci, and from there we proceeded towards Hajvazi. We were supposed to attack Hajvazi and to kill the Serb population there, all of them, in order to free the corridor between Tuzla, Kalesija, Miljanovci, and Hajvazi, to free the passage to Zvornicka Kamenica that was at the time held by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So what happened in Hajvazi? How did you fare?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: In Hajvazi, when we arrived there, the first night one of our soldiers from the 16th Muslim Brigade was killed. He had kept a diary. He recorded who killed whom, who slit whose throat. He was killed that night, not by the Serbs but by somebody else, I don't know who. From there we proceeded in the morning. We started deploying at dawn and we proceeded towards (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: up to 1998 or 1999, on account of a false information that I had been killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 3, or rather, line 5 to line 10, can that be redacted. If you agree, I believe that this should indeed be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you engage in Hajvazi? Did you manage to take Hajvazi?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: We collected our dead and we returned to - what's it called? - a village near Kalesija. We buried them there and then we returned to Haj -- Zvornicka Kamenica. There was some killings there, we captured some Serbs. Taran and his brother Kobra killed those Serbs. I had to pull them into high grass. Taran had told me to bury them. I didn't want to dig holes. I just dragged them over there some 10 or 15 metres away. I asked some people to go to that sector to find them because I didn't believe that somebody came and collect their bodies, but we didn't get the approval to go there to that location. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many Serbs were killed? Were they killed in fighting or had they been arrested?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Mr. President, they were on a horse and a cart. There were five or six of them. One had a semi-automatic rifle. Taran Osmanovic and his brother Kobra arrested them. They jumped on them immediately. We had to obey their rules, and then they killed those five men. A group of people came out of a streamlet, including women, and they told us that they had arrived from Srebrenica, that they were Muslims. Among them there were women and men, and Taran ordered us to kill them, that they should not be allowed to say what had happened to the previous five men. So we did that, and again I had to drag those bodies with some other lads who were with me. We had to drag those bodies. We were supposed to bury them in holes, but I never wanted to bury those men. He shouted at me, asking me why I wouldn't do that. I couldn't, I just couldn't. I pleaded -- I still plead with the International Tribunal to allow us to go to Hajvazi to that location and then you will gain the best picture of what had happened there, because the Federation never allowed us to go there to that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were those really Muslims, these civilians?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Mr. President, they claimed they were going from Srebrenica and they were Muslims, but all they had on them were photographs, no passports, no IDs, and no evidence, no proof. It wasn't like a woman could produce an ID and say: I'm Ajsa. Some were wearing Turkish pantaloons, another was wearing Muslim clothing. But even if they had had IDs to prove they were Muslims, they would still have been killed by Taran in order to prevent this story from spreading about who had killed the previous five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many were these civilians?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: That was the first group. Are we talking about the first group at Hajvazi? Two women and three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the real name of this Taran?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Adil Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did your unit go after that?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: We returned from there to Miljanovci, and there we get orders to go again to Neza -- Nezuh. In Nezuh we spent a few days waiting for a guide whose nickname was Ninja. After a couple of days, he took us to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened in Konjevic Polje, who did you meet with? Or did you join anyone, and who was leading you at that point in the 16th?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade, when they came from Nezuk with this Ninja guide, we were there for a while as the 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade, not long, until Naser and Zulfo Tursun came, accompanied by Amir, and they held a meeting in Konjevic Polje in the schoolhouse. Nurif Rizvanovic took out a yellow envelope there and handed it to Naser. When Naser saw from that paper that Rizvanovic was supposed to be the commander all the way to Bijeljina, that he would be like the Commander-in-Chief in that area, Naser didn't agree with it and Zulfo Tursun didn't agree with it, so they scheduled another meeting to be held in Srebrenica. A couple of days later, the orders came that we were going to Srebrenica for that meeting and it was in the Hotel Domavija. They couldn't come to an agreement there either. It was decided that we, the 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade, under the command of Nurif Rizvanovic would have as our area the area up to Konjevic Polje, and the rest would be under Naser. And the agreement reached at that meeting was that we would help each other out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry, Mr. Witness, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know much English, very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you can wear the headphones again. Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber wanted to know where we were heading. Through this -- it's a bit difficult to follow this line of evidence. Can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Your Excellencies. What I want is to put to the Trial Chamber the atmosphere with all its military and civilian aspects, from Zvornik to Zepa, then we will be moving on from 1993 to 1995, to see who the people were who were in command there. We'll do it very briefly, we'll see what was going on, who was killing whom, and then we will move on to the crisis in 1993 and then the crisis in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one thing. It may be that there's a need for a redaction at lines 11 to 12 of page 70. It's a matter for the Defence and Your Honours, of course, but just highlighting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Duly noted. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And we could also redact, perhaps, the information provided by Mr. Robinson about where the witness had lived for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd appreciate it if you could do this briefly. Let us just concentrate on what happened and then move on to 1993. What happened with your unit and with Nurif Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: You mean very briefly, after that meeting in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, no details. Just the events. This happened, that happened. How was this disagreement between Rizvanovic and Naser Oric resolved?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The agreement when we came was for us to attack that village. Nurif Rizvanovic and the 16th Muslim Brigade, assisted by Naser Oric and Zulfo Tursun and other units, we attacked Siljkovici, but they didn't help us. And we immediately lost ground because Naser stabbed us in the back, spreading stories among the people: You see what kind of army this is, they were not able to get into Kravica. And then what happened next in Srebrenica, we, the 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade, all the able-bodied people in Srebrenica, who were suffering shortages of food, et cetera, et cetera, we were supposed to help them to go to Tuzla. We agreed. Commander Rizvanovic and Tursun promised to help us, and we, the 16th Muslim Eastern Brigade, were supposed to take these people to Tuzla. We agreed. When the people gathered and when we headed from Konjevic Polje across Cerska, Redzici, Bajrici, Zvornicka Kamenica, when we reached Crni Vrh, we had Motorolas, we had a radio that belonged to us, the 16th Brigade. There was the second incident of back-stabbing. Naser called the Serbs and told them that 3.000 Mujahedin were coming to attack them, and then a plane came and started bombing us with some incendiary ammunition and the Serbian army started defending that road thinking that we were the Mujahedin and we were about to attack Zvornik. A lot of men got killed there. One part of our column managed to get through, and the first commander at the head of that column was Velid Sabic. One group of the people managed to get through with him, and the rest of us were engulfed in battle between Crni Vrh and Gornja Kamenica. It was a very difficult situation. They were coming at us from all sides, but we managed to get out. But still we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you speak more slowly so that everything is recorded. What kind of losses did you suffer and what happened with those bodies?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, Karadzic, we had losses and people from our unit were buried in Zvornicka Kamenica. We had losses but I don't know exactly how many, but lots of us were killed and some of the people who were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did somebody later bury them to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I don't know about those people, ordinary people, who were following us. After that we came to Konjevic Polje, and then a couple of days later news came from Srebrenica. An attack followed at Ilino Brdo and Cerska. Again, the 16th Brigade with Nurif Rizvanovic were supposed to be there for the next couple of days to await that attack. Nurif was wearing a jumper and camouflage pants. A lot of local residents from Cerska were getting killed, and again -- how can a sniper hit a civilian in a trench and cannot hit Nurif Rizvanovic? So that back-stabbing campaign started again. Nurif Rizvanovic is not being targeted by the Serbs, et cetera, et cetera. We had two cousins from Bijeljina, we call them the diesel guys. Out of those two cousins, two were killed and another man were killed from Bratunac. After those seven days when we were waiting for that attack at Ilino Brdo and trying to defend ourselves, during that attack Zulfo Tursun and Naser Oric came to Konjevic Polje. Naser Oric went to Cerska and Zulfo Tursun stayed with his men there. They arrested Rizvanovic and attacked us because we were allegedly attacking our own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are talking too fast. So what happened? He was arrested and taken to Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Nurif Rizvanovic, when he was arrested, he was locked up the first seven days in Konjevic Polje, in a warehouse, where there is a petrol station now. There was a shop there at the time. Naser came and Zulfo Tursunovic promised that he would be tried in Srebrenica. Zulfo Tursun and another man who drove a motor cultivator took him from there, passed through Konjevic Polje, and liquidated him somewhere near Sandici. Nobody knows to this day where his body is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell me briefly what happened with your unit after the murder of Nurif Rizvanovic?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: A couple of days later, an offer was made to us to go where we wanted to go to Srebrenica. Some went to Srebrenica. I went personally to join the independent battalion in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many losses did you have at Ilino Brdo and who buried these people?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Seven. These people from Cerska, they had their own workers' platoon that picked up the wounded and the dead, but where they took them I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many casualties?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: In my unit, the 16th Muslim Brigade, we lost 15 to 20 pieces --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've been going for quite some time now, and I am struggling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- to see the relevance of most of this testimony, in particular the detail. I struggle to see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I asked the question. It's up to you how to use your time, but it's inappropriate to delve into such detail while background may be relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. This witness waited for ten years to tell someone the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so it's difficult for me to stop him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- inappropriate comment, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just repeating what he said when he made the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you tell us, what did your battalion hold in the meantime? Why did it stop holding what it was holding and where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: At that time we were deployed in Konjevic Polje along lines. By that time I had joined the Independent Mountain Battalion in Glogova, and I held the line from Burnice village near Previla hill, until an order came from Srebrenica, from Ejub Golic, that everybody who had joined the independent battalion and all the Glogova residents should gather together to get Glogova back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you manage, and until what time did you defend it?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, we recaptured Glogova and managed to defend it all the way until 1993, mid-April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's much better when you answer briefly. And where did you go then and why?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Then I moved to Srebrenica because Naser had come to Glogova several times. We didn't want to leave Glogova, we had lost 150 of our men there, and it was hard for us to decide to leave Glogova. And Naser came five or six times, begging us to leave Glogova. He promised us better treatment in Srebrenica, and it's true to this day that the men from Glogova were the best fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were you during the Serb counter-offensive on Srebrenica and were you in Srebrenica when General Morillon was there visiting? And were you able, and from what distance, to follow, to observe, his visit?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: In 1993, when the Serbs attacked Srebrenica, from Kragljivode, from -- until that hill, I participated in all that until they told us the UNPROFOR was coming. At that point, I went to Srebrenica. We had our own special command for our men from Glogova, and I found myself close to Morillon and Naser Oric, when he held that speech from the window of the post office building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see you in that footage where Morillon is holding a speech?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes. I was watching one of the cases here in The Hague when this footage was shown, and I watched it again when I was in prison. Again, this same footage we saw a moment ago in the case of -- I don't remember which trial it was. And from that time I kept writing to the International Tribunal in The Hague, that I was not dead, that I was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope the Prosecution will give us that letter you wrote. And did you have occasion to be close to Naser Oric after you moved to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of times. And I spoke to him, I had two meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown, without broadcasting, 1D9584. And could the witness be given the electronic pen, please, the Stylus. This is not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark yourself with an arrow and Naser Oric as well.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: That's him. Take the footage from before, shave that face, and you will be able to compare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Put number 1 next to Naser Oric and 2 next to yourself.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this taken?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: When we arrived in the centre of Kravica. This large building used to be a shop before the war. It's in the centre of Kravica. This does not exist anymore because a monument has been erected in this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What date was it?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: 7 January 1993. Sometime afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please place HV12 [as interpreted] in the bottom of the photograph and today's date.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: W, all right.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Today's date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think today's the 9th, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please be admitted under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives document number D4181, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D9585, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, if I may just say something about this photograph because there's a man here whom I know and who is something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please return it so that the witness may, if the Chamber allows the witness to clarify this. But again, please do not broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that this man here whom you can see -- can we manage this, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Stylus has not been activated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not activated. I need this man because of a grave in Kragljivode.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He would know where the grave in Kragljivode was. Whose grave is it?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: It's in the statement, once we get to that today or tomorrow, when the attack on Kragljivode was launched, when the Serbs and Russians were taken prisoners and buried and the grave is not there. It has not been found to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has been moved?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: We have been in the field a metre or a metre and a half to it but it has gone missing. It was all one grave next to the other. This man, today he's the main man in charge of the graves, he searches for them. He's the main man today and I had problems with him when I came to my town, to my native town, in 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just go into private session for a minute to hear his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know his name. I just know that he's from Voljavac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we don't need to do that. Now, if we can see the other document first. But, excuse me, if we can add this to the previous number, please. No, it's unnecessary. All right. Fine. 1D9585, please. That one should also not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you be seen in this photograph? We can see Naser. Can you just circle yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Well, I can't even recognise myself. That's what the photograph is like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can't recognise yourself?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I can't recognise myself here because the photograph is all somehow like this, the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll survive with just the one that we already had. Okay. Now I would ask you if you can, as briefly as possible, tell us how many actions Naser launched against the Serbian villages between the place when the protected zone was declared and 1995, July 1995?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There was an action in 1994 when we went up to help Gorazde, and from there the troops were collected in Srebrenica and then they went to help those at their back. How can I explain to the Chamber and you and everyone? We had some sort of demobilisation [as interpreted] at the time. Nobody touched us. No one shot at us, no one was attacking us. But it was decided then and we went up there, I have a witness for that also, who is now in the Foca penal and correctional facility. We met once. We saw one another and were introduced. That was during this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 25, I believe that you said "demilitarisation," rather than "demobilisation"; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, that demote zone as it was saying on the boards at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other actions in surrounding villages that you were aware of when you went out into the Serbian villages and outside from the protected zone?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There was that one and it was said that the -- the headquarters should be blown up, and once there was an ambush in -- near Crni Vrh, close to Zvornicka Kamenica, where some police and military troops were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you now please tell us, what was the road travelled by your unit and you personally from the 11th of July in the evening up -- and then the first night and the second night and the first day and the second night and the second day, when did you start withdrawing and did you start withdrawing? Did you leave as a unit? Can you tell us as briefly as possible how did that go, who made the decision and where did you leave? Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Just briefly, on the 10th of July, 1995, under the command of Ejub Golic, who was killed, and with Zulfo Tursun, who had a conversation about money, the money didn't arrive in time, it was not distributed, only to the independent mountain battalion. And we left the front. We set off in the direction of Srebrenica. We reached our command in Srebrenica, where it was. We burnt our papers. Then we set out from there and we reached the UNPROFOR base, and there a guard, as there was a guard-house that was quite high, perhaps 3 metres, and there was one guard who was at the gate and one who was there, they didn't allow us to enter. And one guard was killed, he was a Dutch man, and the other one was wounded. We then broke inside. We collected our weapons which had been seized from us as early as in 1993 when the UNPROFOR came and -- the Canadians at first and then those Dutchmen also. We collected our weapons. We boarded them on to a truck and with the truck we came above a village which stretches from the graveyard in Kazani up until Fojari, the village that's on the right-hand side. I'm not sure what the name of the area is. From there we transported the weapons to Cumavici, where we would need to be reviewed. Whoever did not have a rifle was given one. And the people who left from there, who wanted to go with the battalion was going together with us. From there we went down to Lehovici. From Lehovici we reached Susnjari --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that there was a troop review in Cumavici; correct?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who made the decision that all the 28th Division should be sent towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I don't think there was evidence to that effect yet. That's a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I shall rephrased it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did it happen that the entire 28th Division should leave Srebrenica and set out from there?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: We from the independent mountain battalion, from Glogova under the command of Ejub Golic left the line, from Zeleni Jadar and the Tabla hill all the way to another big hill whose name I didn't know, we were holding the line but we didn't get the money as promised by Zulfo Tursun, and we didn't get the money that came from Sarajevo in the helicopter that crashed. They were supposed to distribute 100 Deutschemarks to every soldier, but one hodza and one woman went to Serbia. They got caught there. They never distributed the money to us, and we abandoned the front line. Nobody wanted to defend Srebrenica for free and have other people get rich at our expense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know about the others? Did all the brigade that were part of the 28th Division move towards there?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: All of us, as we were going back from Tabla hill towards Srebrenica, all the people from the houses also set out in the direction of the centre of Srebrenica town. And then all of the people, one group from Potocari, UNPROFOR via Susnjari to Buljim, all of us got together in Susnjari, the commands, and that was the place where we rallied. And the people were moving towards Buljim and Tuzla because everyone had been told that we would be moving towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how you fared during the first night. As briefly as possible, just list for us what were all the things that happened during the first night as you set out and initiated a breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: During the first night when we started, Ejub Golic was next to me, there was one young man we called Rambo, a relative of Ejub Golic, and there was Kezo also, who was the commander of the 2nd Company of the 2nd Battalion and the Mountain Battalion. And we were the last to set off in terms of Buljim in the direction of Tuzla. The column had moved before us. When we came down to a brook, from Buljim, once we reached this brook, then an oak fell down rather than an elm, as I have been hearing the witnesses say here for years, and this oak had carvings on it made by a knife or a small axe and it had been set on fire. It fell 5 metres in front of us. When it fell down, people started shooting. It was the Serbs shooting from the direction of Sandici. And from their Pragas and their APCs, they fired. And on the left-hand side, as we were moving from the direction of Srebrenica, we got engaged. We went up the hill because there was a hill on the right-hand side, from Kravica to Sandici, and on the left-hand side we mounted the hill, as you can see, that's the Rogac hill. So we held this hill during that night because the Serbian army was down there. There's a field down there in the road. When they saw that we had mounted before them and started shooting against them, then they couldn't mount the hill because there was too much clear ground. And in the morning I saw -- let me not mention any numbers, but I saw perhaps around 100 bodies from Buljim down there. What I would like to explain to the Chamber now, there at Buljim, there weren't so many casualties as in Burnice, at the very entrance to Burnice, the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the same night or --

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just help us now, please. These 100 bodies, did you bury them or take them away with you or were they left there for somebody else to bury them?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: No one touched them. You were just looking their back-packs whether they had any ammunition. If I told someone that I had found 100.000 Deutschemarks --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you repeat from what -- from where you referred to 100.000 Deutschemarks? And speak slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you do with 100.000 Deutschemarks?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I smoked them, I rolled them into cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpretation is wrong. You didn't roll them, but you rolled tobacco into them?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: That was my paper for cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And during that day was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Mr. President, we didn't fight at all until we reached the Kaldrmica Put and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. So on the following night --

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There was an ambush at the entrance of Burnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A Serbian ambush?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe to the Chamber what happened on the second night?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: When the people were killed, we passed over these bodies, that was between two hills and a big wide building was erected there. A woman and a man from Konjevic Polje wanted to have a chicken farm there, and that was where the ambush was made and a mass of dead were there and then we passed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who shot on the second night? Who was shooting at whom?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The second night was Kaldrmica, down there. Once we reached the village Burnice, the village Burnice. And when we reached a graveyard Burnice, then there was the whole brigade, Zulfo Tursun to the left from Novo Kasaba. We from Glogova would go straight. And the remaining companies, and so on, there were three possible roads: Nova Kasaba, ones would go there, Zulfo Tursun would go with them. Us from Glogova would go towards the road Kaldrmica-Konjevic Polje, which crosses Milici. And a third group would go from Taran's cafe restaurant and the bridge, there was a bridge there. The third group was supposed to attack there because it was reported to us that Serbs were there under the fly-over and that they were waiting to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many casualties were there during the second night and did you bring them with you or did you bury them?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There were casualties along the bridge, in Kaldrmica, but the casualties were people who were shooting from Taran's cafe restaurant in Konjevic Polje and from this hill whose name I don't know above Nova Kasaba, the first hill, and they were shooting from there. But there weren't too many bodies as for that when we broke through the front line, because I'm moving on from there to the Tumac [phoen] hill. And the Tumac hill is on the right-hand side when going in the direction of Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And which bodies did you have to go over? Whose bodies were there and when were they killed on your entry into Kaldrmica that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: These were Muslim bodies on the bridge -- excuse me, just hold your horses. The bodies in Burnice, the ambush, these were the Muslim bodies, we had to step over them, we could not pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many bodies were there?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number, but there was quite a number of them, quite a few of them. What I can testify is that when I left Srebrenica and Buljim, one ambush, two ambushes, breaking through the front line, reaching Crni Vrh, reaching close to Nezuk, going back, I can just confirm that I could see between 15- and 1700 dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did you spend the third night?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: When I went to Udrc and we reached it, then I was going back along the road because we couldn't pass. Then I returned again, and that would be the 13th in the morning. I hid in a grave, concrete grave, I hid there and in the morning as I was getting out, a man, a Serb, a soldier threw a rifle down because he was so afraid. There was another one who aimed his rifle at me and he said: How come that you're coming out of there? And that was when nobody beat me, nobody did nothing to me there. We left there. I went to Kravica. 24 of them in front of me, I was the 25th, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will get to that. Please tell us whether there were any losses from friendly fire, as it's usually called, among the Muslims, I mean, once you split into these three columns?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Well, there were murders, Mr. Karadzic, and everyone else in the courtroom, there were people who got killed because once the shooting started, groups would be formed, three, four, or five of us who knew each other would form a group. We were one group. Then somebody else would come along. He didn't have, for example, his military ID. Then you would kill him on the spot if he didn't have a personal ID. Such things did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why were there such killings?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: We didn't trust anyone anymore, the world, the people, not yourself, you wouldn't trust yourself even in such a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there killings out of confusion during the night when darkness fell?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, every night there would be -- somebody would shout: The Chetniks are coming, shoot, shoot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. All those are leading questions which would reduce the probative value of this witness's evidence. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to see somebody surrendering, to whom? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: In Sandici some people were taken prisoners. Those who were killed in Konjevic Polje. Nurif Rizvanovic's brother Huso wore a white shirt and he invited people to surrender. He guaranteed people that nothing would happen to them and people did surrender. I don't know where these people are who killed him. I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you see them after their surrender?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I passed between the villages of Kamenica. Here in the International Criminal Tribunal nobody knew that there was Kamenica Pobudjka, the only story was about Zvornik. From Kamenica to Kravica there is about 10 to 20 minutes on foot and from the hilltop you can see Sandici where people had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see those people in Sandici? How many were there in Sandici according to you?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: According to my estimate, in Sandici, I really can't say how many there were, perhaps about 250 to 300 people all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were taken by Sandici, you had already been arrested?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were you taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One clarification. Minutes ago you said, for example, anybody of the group did not have, for example, his military ID, then you would kill him on the spot if he didn't have his ID. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I stand by it. Judge, if I don't know you and if I tell you stop and you stop and I ask you where you're from and then you say a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did you not say today before that you all burnt your papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the independent mountain battalion, we burned the papers belonging to the people. We didn't want the Serbs to find our names, we didn't know them -- to know them how many fighters they -- there were, because we knew that all of our names had already been sent to Tuzla. We burnt everything in our command, all the orders at that command. We did not want to leave anything to the Serbs, to Ratko Mladic. We didn't want them to know what we had done. If you were a member of a unit, you had to have a military booklet. It was a blue booklet with your name, your photo, and the white lily on the cover. And if I did not see that, I kill -- I would kill you immediately. Even if you were my mother, I wanted to save my hide and that's why I'm here. I was more than a slave and now I know more than I was supposed to know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please be asked not to overlap and allow for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You should put a pause yourself. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I need to be reminded of that more than the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you didn't burn your IDs?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: We did not burn our military booklets. We burned the orders, all the other documents. For example, there were papers on which it said Husic Huso went somewhere and killed two, and those strategic places, there were maps drawn for the people to show them where they had to go. We burnt all that, all about the operations that took place between 1992 and 1993. As for the military booklets, each of the soldiers had to have one on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the assumption, if somebody didn't have those documents why was he supposed to be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused be asked not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your answer. Start over from the beginning -- from the outset.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to repeat about the burning of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Why were the -- did they risk being killed if they did not have their military booklets? What was the assumption?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Well, I had several such cases where I had to act to save my life. For example, if they didn't know the code, you would kill them. Some of them we stripped to see whether they had been circumcised. You killed them, although later on it would turn out that the person was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that they were not circumcised?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes. The times were such that you couldn't say I'm Huso Husic from Osmace. I needed to see a document to prove you were who you say you were. And then when they say: Well, I left them in Srebrenica, I couldn't care less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On line 13 you said the names of some Muslim players, instead of that we see the word "code." What is Bismillah, can you tell that to the Chamber and the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Bismillah Surah is something from the Qur'an. It's a prayer that every Muslim child learns when are they at the age of three or four. It's a very common basic Muslim prayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when the 25 of you were brought to Kravica, can you tell us, very shortly but very accurately, what happened there?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: When we entered Kravica, on the left-hand side I saw some people sitting there. There were two openings, and we proceeded to the entrance on the right-hand side. At that moment, a person from Kravica who knew me and my mother, he knew me and he asked me what I was doing there, and then I said: Well, you see I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Don't say his name, we are in open session --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he took me to the office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just noting, I'm afraid I didn't stand up fast enough because of the interpreting, but there was a leading question, "and when the 25 of you were brought to Kravica," there's been nothing about 25 people during the evidence. It's just repeating these leading questions throughout this latter part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, where did these 25 people come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it wasn't recorded it's a problem. The witness is speaking fast and so am I, but the witness did say: There were 24 of us plus me and it took us about 10 to 15 minutes to arrive in Kravica. This is what the witness did say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's on page 86, lines 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Please put a pause. It's almost impossible to catch up such speed on the part of the interpreters. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Continue. You said that a man, a friend of yours, recognised you. Can you now tell us the sequence of events in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: He told me to go to a room. I opened the door. I entered. The room was small and there was another room adjacent to it, and I heard short bursts of fire and I jumped through the window and I just split. I disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people were there, according to your estimate, who were killed and how many of them were in the left room, those who had arrived before you?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: According to my estimate, a minimum in the left room were about 70 to 80 people. Those rooms could not hold 100 or 200 people. Those were two small rooms and there was a partition between the two of them. Can I have some water, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you see something? On top of hearing things.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see anything. I couldn't see whether those men from my group were killed. I couldn't see anything. I only know that I saw a video-clip. It was shown on TV, mostly by Sarajevo television, and namely I was wrote about --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that I could see people lying on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: If it's the case that the witness is about to testify to what he watched subsequently on TV, I really struggle to see how this could assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Move on or reformulate your question. Probably if you want to ask something specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- those men and I saw them on TV --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because they were in my group and I saw them on TV on that video-clip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wait for the question. Just both do not overlap. Just wait. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After you heard those shots, did you subsequently learn what had happened to your colleagues who had been brought together with you and how did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I learned what I just tried to tell you. When I escaped, I came across a man whose name was Enver, and he claimed that he had been in Kravica and that he escaped from there. And because of him, six lads had been sentenced to 40 years in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When I researched that case and I provided a statement to the prosecutor's office, I can give you the name of the person to whom I provided that statement. When I provided that statement, he did not call me to testify. He threatened me and told me that I was not supposed to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the question was: "After you heard the shots, did you subsequently learn what had happened to your colleagues who had been brought together with you and how did you learn that?" Did we hear the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just given you the answer. I learned from a man or from people who were there that everybody in Kravica had been killed, and I learned that in 2008 or 2009, for God's sake. What I saw previously in 1997, 1998, I saw that on BH television and airs that programme and claims that 1500 to 2000 men were killed. When I met that colleague of mine - and I can tell you about the case that was heard before a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina - the Skelanci case and those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said. Speak very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, listen and understand what I'm saying. You have a group in the prosecutor's office on the prosecution team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you don't understand. Unfortunately, I do not understand your language. I hear from the interpreters interpretation. If you speak so fast, it's impossible for them to interpret. So please speak slowly. They didn't hear your last answer. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Skelanci, the Skelanci group and then continue from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there was a trial involving six guys from Skelani, alleging that they had participated in the killings of 1500 to 2000 Muslims in Kravica, I was in a different kind of life. I was in a political life, and those politicians from the Federation, not from Republika Srpska, appointed me to that position. And then I saw in the newspapers that there was a trial and I recognised those men on TV. And on the following morning, I got up and I wrote a letter to the prosecutor's office in Sarajevo, asking them for somebody from the prosecutor's office to visit me because I wanted to give them my statement about those lads. And when I did provide a statement, when I started telling them my story about the cases that I'm telling you about today, one of the prosecutors took me to the bathroom in the place where I was and I told -- and he told me not to mention Naser Oric or others from that unit. I was supposed to testify on behalf of those lads, and the other guy testified, that one that I found when I jumped through the window in Kravica. Enver is his name. He said that he was there, that he saw everything, that he had been wounded in the lower leg, and that's the guy who I found on the hilltop. He was the key witness and still they got 37, 38, or even 40 years each. I was promised from there that people would come from the court to take me to court, nobody came, nobody wanted to come and pick me up. And when the lads came to me, when I started to socialise with them, when I gave them the papers, when they saw what I had done for them, and I was supposed to be there on their behalf, people almost killed each other, because I -- the others had threatened me for what I wanted to do for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please pause there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has difficulty in understanding or in following this part, so could you -- Mr. Karadzic, could you break down so that the witness can state what he wants to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I'll give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, after you fled from the co-operative, from the office, can you describe very briefly where you were and what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I ran away, I ran through the woods, I lived in the woods, managing ten minutes -- ten months passed between that and the arrest. Everybody understands here in the international forum that I was under their protection. What do they call it? ICTY. But still my own people sent me into prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were in hiding for ten months?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause, please. Put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now you said you were in hiding in the woods for ten months. Were you alone? Were you in a group? And was it the only group in those ten months?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: That group that I met, that was in Zvornicka Kamenica. With that group I came back to Srebrenica, to Lehovici. That group remained there, and I joined some other people and went to Zepa. In that other group, there were another six people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When were you captured again?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: 30th May 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did they know about you and how?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: When I was brought - can I say where I was brought? - to Zvornik, to the police, the police interrogated me and they accused me that I killed four Serbs and one Muslim out of that group of seven who were arrested before the 10th of May. So they put it all on me, they blamed it all on me, and it was up to me to defend myself from these charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, arrested by who, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you prosecuted and tried and what happened later?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I was tried based on their allegations. There was no evidence. And from 1996 to date, there are no bodies, no rifle. These are the people killed, the four Serbs, and they blamed it on me. There was an Interpol arrest warrant for one of them, for that guy who was sent to Switzerland. He got 20 years in prison for killing those four people in Zepa. That's a political game being played now in the Federation. We were being portrayed as heros, people who couldn't do that, but they could and they did, 100 per cent. There is somebody in the Federation of BH who's protecting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said the Mothers of Srebrenica and the SDA were protecting them?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The SDA, Sulejman Tihic, Bakira, the woman from Mothers of Srebrenica, they keep protecting them and they keep trying to prove that they are innocent. But they can't know better than me and that's why I'm in everybody's way, in the way of the Muslims and Republika Srpska because Muslims on one side know their own truth, the Serbs know another, and they're all playing a game of -- a political game of tug of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that you got out of the Serb prison?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: There was an exchange. It could have been the 22nd or the 24th of May, 1997. An exchange was agreed for one captain who had been captured in Sarajevo and I together with three others were supposed to be exchanged for him. He was to continue serving his sentence in Republika Srpska, whereas I was supposed to go on serving my ten-year sentence in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you were in prison in Republika Srpska or in the Federation, were you prepared to state your own truth?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Back in 1996 I told the prison warden and I wrote letters everywhere that they enable me to come to the international tribunal. At that time it was a well-known fact there was an international tribunal in The Hague and I wrote letters among other people to the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you try to get in touch later with someone from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Only after 2008 or 2009.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D9587 is the next document I would like to call up in e-court without broadcasting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would like you to stop for today at 2.40.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you remember, to whom did you write this letter and when?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately we still don't have a translation. Perhaps the OTP has a translation because it's their document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I think we do. We were only informed that this would be used, obviously, a few hours ago. But if I can just consult with my colleague, I can see whether it can be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what are you telling the prosecutor's office of Bosnia-Herzegovina here, that you have some information?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you equally prepared to talk about the civilian losses on both sides or only on one side?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and everyone in the courtroom, that's the letter that I sent when the prosecutor came to Foca and threatened me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it will assist, this could be shown with the Prosecution's 65 ter number which is 25496, and there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Shall we upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read until we get the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "Dear gentlemen, I also know the exact dates and perpetrators of the heinous crimes committed against innocent civilian population on the territory of Srebrenica, Kravica, Sase, Loznicka Rijeka, Skelani municipalities." Who lived in Sase, Loznicka Rijeka, and Skelani?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: In Kravica there was a majority Serb population. In Skelani, the Serbs were -- at least in the surrounding villages there was a majority of Serbs until perhaps Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Loznicka Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: As far as I know, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was your unit involved in the attack on the Fakovici village?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: We were in Fakovici to lend a hand -- I mean we from the independent mountain battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the BH prosecutor's office to your letter where you express your readiness to shed light on these crimes?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: I'm now addressing the Judges and you, Mr. Karadzic, and the Prosecutors. When I sent this letter, people from the Federation came to see me, two prosecutors, and one woman, they recorded everything I said. When I was supposed to go Sarajevo to be called as a witness at the trial, I received very threatening messages from one man who sent this message through an intermediary, and I have that witness whom I can call, that man approached me and told me how things stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was the prosecutor who visited you in Foca and threatened you?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: The name? Bajro Kulovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did Bajro Kulovac's career progress?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Bajro Kulovac was a prosecutor. I don't know what happened with him. I know that I had another encounter with him in 2010 because this -- this occurred in 2008. And in 2010 I ended up at his mercy again. Naser Oric was there, the president of the SDA, lawyer Damir Alagic, they were the top people in the Federation. This Bajro Kulovac tried to break my limbs. He wanted me to sign a paper stating that I did not suffer anything in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say you were at his mercy, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Damir Alagic, a lawyer from Sarajevo, brought me to SIPA, to the office of Bajro Kulovac, and they put to me papers, saying that I wasn't in Srebrenica, I know nothing about Srebrenica. Then I asked Bajro Kulovac: Why did you send those innocent men to prison when they were not guilty? He said: I have the bullets, I have the bodies, I have the bones. I said: Well, anybody could have found them in the woods. And then he slapped me so hard I fell off the chair. Then in the presence of Damir Alagic I was taken to the office of the boss in SIPA for an interview, when they asked me - and maybe you know about that case too - when he asked me if I had given that statement under coercion or of my own will, when I was about to say, "Of my own will," Damir Alagic hit me. Because Damir Alagic, the lawyer, didn't want to talk to that Serb who was the chief of SIPA at that time. He wanted to talk to his own man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 20, they asked you to say you did not suffer anything in Srebrenica, but in fact they wanted you to sign that you had never been in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Yes, they wanted me to sign that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember your warning about the time, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did they ask that? In 2010, Amor Masovic told me in the presence of my father that it would have been better for me to have kept my mouth shut and be still recorded as missing because in that cases they wouldn't be looking for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit this letter under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document receives Exhibit Number D4182, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we'll continue tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just can I make one correction in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that Amor Masovic told you that you had -- it would have been better for you to stay dead because you were already recorded as dead?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the last sentence be redacted. Fortunately enough, the father's name has not been recorded so no redaction is necessary, but the audio can be redacted, i.e., it doesn't have to be broadcast right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean I'm not supposed to talk to anybody I know? Who am I not supposed to talk to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's okay to talk to anybody, but you are not supposed to discuss about your testimony. Now do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not before your testimony is over.

utterances.speaker: KW12
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the remaining time, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the accused's requested -- accused's request which was filed on the 6th of December, 2013, that counsel for Ljubisa Beara, Mr. John Ostojic, be present in the courtroom during Beara's testimony. This request is granted. Further, the Chamber has also considered the suggestion raised by the accused and endorsed orally by the Prosecution on the 6th of December in relation to Beara and Tolimir, that in light of the uncertainties surrounding their testimony, their cross-examination be postponed until after the winter recess. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution should be ready to cross-examine Beara and Tolimir, who were indicted respectively in 2002 and 2005; however, given the exceptional timing and circumstances, the Chamber is minded to exercise a degree of flexibility. This request is therefore granted and the Chamber wishes to note that the binding effects of the subpoenas issued respectively against Beara and Tolimir will continue to have effect until the completion of their testimony. Finally, the Chamber will issue an oral ruling on the accused's motion for access to audio recordings from Kvocka case filed on the 9th of December, 2013, wherein the accused requests access to the B/C/S audio recordings of the testimony of Pero Rendic in the Kvocka case for the purpose of preparing the Rule 92 ter attestation procedure. The Prosecution notified the Chamber via e-mail on the 9th of December, 2013, that it did not wish to respond to the motion. The motion is granted and the Chamber hereby orders the Registry to grant the accused access to the B/C/S audio recordings of the testimony of Pero Rendic in the Kvocka case on the 5th of February, 2001. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 10th day of December, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.45 p.m.,
